system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-10-20 13:35:00 to 2156-10-26 09:59:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening abdominal pain and constipation. She had severe epigastric pain radiating to the right side, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with no relief from her usual oral Dilaudid. Labs showed leukocytosis and mild metabolic abnormalities. Imaging confirmed appropriate GJ tube placement without obstruction. She was treated with IV fluids, pain control using scheduled IV Dilaudid, and initiation of oral naloxone for opioid-induced constipation, which led to a successful bowel movement. She advanced to clear liquids and tolerated tube feeds. A Code Purple occurred when she attempted to take unauthorized pills, leading to sedation with Ativan and Zyprexa. Antibiotics for mild G-tube site erythema were discontinued after reassessment. Her insulin regimen was continued without change. She was discharged home with an aggressive bowel regimen, clear instructions on pain management, and follow-up plans.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had this squeezing pain in my belly again—right in the middle and upper part. It woke me up at night. I’ve also been throwing up and having diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the pain different from your usual abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels similar to past times, but it’s been really bad. I’ve had a fever, night sweats, and I haven’t been able to eat much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your blood sugar was high when you arrived—397—and there were ketones in your urine. That means your diabetes is under stress right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I’ve been thirsty and peeing a lot too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are classic signs of high blood sugar. We’ve already given you some insulin to help bring it down. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the pain? It’s really hard to deal with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it with IV fluids and IV Dilaudid for pain. We’re also giving you Compazine for nausea. You’re not eating right now, so we’re holding your tube feeds temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being NPO. When can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids once your nausea and pain improve. It might take a day or two. We want to make sure your stomach can handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had this before—sometimes it’s my gastroparesis acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your history of gastroparesis and chronic pancreatitis makes this tricky. But your lipase level was normal, so it’s probably not a pancreatitis flare this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the diarrhea and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be viral—especially since you had cold symptoms last week. Or it could be related to your diabetes and gut motility. We didn’t get a stool sample, so we can’t confirm infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did have a cough with dark mucus. But I thought it was just a cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. Sometimes a viral illness can trigger gut symptoms like this, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on it. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and adjust your insulin based on your intake. We’ll reassess your pain and nausea every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea isn’t as bad, but I still have some belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs are stable. The urine culture came back with mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination—nothing to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. The results suggest skin or genital bacteria got into the sample. No sign of a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. Can I try some food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And can I take my regular meds by mouth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting your oral meds—metoclopramide, omeprazole, and your pancreatic enzymes. We’ll keep the IV pain meds for now but transition to oral soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been asking for Valium for anxiety. Can I get that more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re limiting IV Valium to avoid over-sedation. You can have your regular oral dose—10mg every 6 hours as needed. Let’s try that first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and soft foods. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I only needed one dose of Dilaudid last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds only—2mg Dilaudid tablet every 4 hours as needed. You’re also back on your full diabetic diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my insulin? Is it the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Lantus dose is staying at 50 units at bedtime. We’re continuing your sliding scale for mealtime insulin based on your blood sugar checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been checking it at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep doing that. We want to make sure your sugars stay in a safer range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days without vomiting or diarrhea. Your pain is well-controlled with oral meds. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s awesome. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular medications. We’re adjusting a few—your Remeron dose is now 15mg at night instead of 30mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still effective for sleep and appetite, but the lower dose reduces drowsiness and weight gain risks. Your Trazodone is also now 100mg instead of 200mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can handle that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow morning. You’ve been off IV meds for over 24 hours, eating regular food, and your blood sugar is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Should I be worried if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your oral Dilaudid as prescribed. If you have vomiting, diarrhea, or can’t keep food down for more than 24 hours, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep checking your blood sugar four times a day. If it’s over 300 twice in a row, or you have ketones, call your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’re alert, walking, and your vitals are stable. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I restart my tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as tolerated. If you’re eating well, you may not need them. But keep them available if your appetite drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. ___ in a few days. They’ll review your meds and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re doing well—pain controlled, no nausea, eating normally. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you at follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, along with elevated blood glucose and ketones. She was treated with IV fluids, insulin, and IV Dilaudid for pain, while being kept NPO initially. Her symptoms improved over several days, allowing transition to oral medications and a regular diabetic diet. The abdominal pain was likely related to her chronic gastroparesis or a post-viral gastrointestinal episode, though pancreatitis was ruled out due to normal lipase. Urine culture showed contamination, not infection. She stabilized psychiatrically, accepted oral medications, and was discharged home in stable condition with medication adjustments and close follow-up planned.
